newsitem.title: USA: Judge to decide Seagram/Viacom remedy in September.
newsitem.headline: Judge to decide Seagram/Viacom remedy in September.

text.p: A Delaware judge said Thursday that unless Seagram Co Ltd and Viacom Inc can negotiate a remedy by September on their USA Networks partnership dispute, he will do it for them.

In May, Vice Chancellor Myron Steele of the Delaware Chancery Court ruled that the existing partnership was no longer "tenable" because Viacom's ownership of the MTV Networks violated a non-compete provision of the original partnership.

USA Networks was formed in 1981 by Time Warner Inc predecessor Time Inc and Viacom predecessor Paramount Communications Inc and was later joined by Universal Studios Inc, which is now an 80 percent owned affiliate of Seagram and had been owned by Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd .
At the end of a two hour hearing, Steele, a duck hunter, issued a cryptic warning to a flock of lawyers who are not.
"If you're in a duck blind and a duck heads toward you 25 feet away and your partner hands you a shotgun, you'd better make sure there's a firing pin before you pull the trigger."

In court documents Seagram has proposed that Viacom trigger a buy-sell option which would allow Seagram to sell its half of the partnership at the high end of a valuation range or buy Viacom's half at the low end.

Universal lawyer Ron Olson told Steele Thursday that Seagram also wanted Viacom to "disgorge" the $180 million in dividends and the increased value of the partnership it has gained since becoming a partner by acquiring Paramount in 1994.

Steele suggested both sides reread his 55 page May ruling to get an idea of what kind of remedy he will come up with. In that ruling Steele ordered both sides to agree on a plan that would discontinue USA Networks in its present form and provide for the disposal of its assets.

He also said the buy-sell provision was "elective, not compulsory." But while noting that "USA Networks is an extremely well run and profitable enterprise," Steele added it would be unfair for Viacom to benefit "at (Seagram's) expense" from operations of the partnership and the competing MTV networks.
In June, negotiations on a consensual plan broke off when Seagram turned down Viacom's offer of $1.94 billion for Seagram's half of the USA Networks.

Seagram attorney Herbert Wachtell said Thursday that because the judge ruled that Viacom breached the partnership contract, it should be barred from continuing to benefit by operating both the MTV and USA networks simultaneously.
He proposed that Viacom find a buyer approved by Seagram, or allow Seagram to buy at the same price. Failing that, "the buy-sell (provision) becomes the exit mechanism," Wachtell said.
Viacom attorney Robert Zimet disagreed and repeated the company's proposal for a public auction of the partnership with the rules to be set by Steele.

"An auction keeps the process honest by allowing all parties to bid and get best value...We're at risk to lose a strategic asset...It would not hurt (Universal) if it did prevail at auction to pay a fair price."
Both sides declined to comment on whether negotiations would be resumed.
